items.followUp: State the two factors that determine the work done by a force.

rubric.why: Work depends on the applied force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying force magnitude as a factor.

rubric.why: Work also depends on the displacement in the force’s direction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying displacement in the direction of the force.

modelAnswer: Work done depends on the magnitude of the force and the displacement of the body in the direction of that force.

items.followUp: Define stress and state its SI unit.

rubric.why: Elasticity describes a material’s recovery after the deforming force is removed.
rubric.description: Defines elasticity as recovery of original shape or size.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the material regains its original shape or size after the deforming force is removed.

rubric.why: Stress is the force acting per unit area.
rubric.description: Defines stress as force per unit area.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition of stress.

modelAnswer: Elasticity is the property of a material by which it regains its original shape and size when the deforming force is removed.
Stress is the force acting per unit area of a body.

items.followUp: What are the lower and upper fixed points on the Celsius scale?

rubric.why: The lower fixed point is defined by melting ice at standard atmospheric pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as the melting point of ice (0 °C) at standard atmospheric pressure.

rubric.why: The upper fixed point is defined by boiling water at standard atmospheric pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as the boiling point of water (100 °C) at standard atmospheric pressure.

modelAnswer: The lower fixed point is the temperature of melting ice at standard atmospheric pressure, which is 0 °C.
The upper fixed point is the temperature of boiling water at standard atmospheric pressure, which is 100 °C.

items.followUp: Starting from Newton’s second law, show that force equals the change in momentum divided by time.

rubric.why: Newton’s second law relates force to the rate of change of momentum.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that force is proportional to the rate of change of momentum.

rubric.why: Acceleration is the change in velocity per unit time.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for using a = (v − u)/t.

rubric.why: Substituting acceleration into F = ma gives the momentum-change expression.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for obtaining F = m(v − u)/t.

rubric.why: The products mv and mu are final and initial momentum.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for showing F = (P_f − P_i)/t.

modelAnswer: By Newton’s second law, force is proportional to the rate of change of momentum.
For a body of constant mass m, initial velocity u and final velocity v, acceleration a = (v − u)/t.
Therefore, F = ma = m(v − u)/t.
Since P_i = mu and P_f = mv, F = (mv − mu)/t = (P_f − P_i)/t.

items.followUp: A car slows uniformly from 72 km h⁻¹ to 36 km h⁻¹ with a retardation of 2 m s⁻². Find the time taken.

rubric.why: The speeds must be expressed in SI units before using the motion equation.
rubric.description: Converts both speeds to m s⁻¹.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for u = 22.2 m s⁻¹ and v = 5.56 m s⁻¹, or equivalent values.

rubric.why: This is the uniform-acceleration equation needed to find time.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for using v = u + at or its rearranged form.

rubric.why: Correct substitution uses the final speed, initial speed and signed acceleration.
rubric.description: Substitutes the values with the correct sign for retardation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct substitution such as t = (5.56 − 22.2)/(−2).

rubric.why: The calculated time is approximately 8.33 seconds.
rubric.description: Gives the time with a suitable unit.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for t ≈ 8.33 s (or equivalent). Award 1 mark if the result is correct but the unit is missing or there is a minor arithmetic error after correct substitution.

modelAnswer: Using v = u + at, t = (v − u)/a.
The train takes approximately 8.3 s.

items.followUp: Define equilibrium and describe the stable, unstable and neutral states of equilibrium.

rubric.why: A body is in equilibrium when the forces acting on it balance.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the resultant force on the body is zero.

rubric.why: A stable body returns to equilibrium after a small displacement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the return to the original equilibrium position after a small displacement.

rubric.why: An unstable body moves farther from equilibrium after a small displacement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing motion farther from the equilibrium position.

rubric.why: A neutral body remains in equilibrium at its new position.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing equilibrium at the new position (or unchanged height).

modelAnswer: A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force acting on it is zero.
In stable equilibrium, a small displacement makes the body return to its original position.
In unstable equilibrium, a small displacement makes the body move farther from its original position.
In neutral equilibrium, a small displacement leaves the body in equilibrium at its new position.

items.followUp: A pump lifts 150 kg of water through 8 m in 12 s. Calculate its power, taking g = 10 m s⁻².

rubric.why: Power is the work done per unit time.
rubric.description: Chooses the power relation and relevant work.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for using P = W/t and W = mgh, or directly P = mgh/t.

rubric.why: The mass, height, time and gravitational field strength must be substituted consistently.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct substitution using m = 200 kg, h = 6 m, t = 10 s and g = 9.8 or 10 m s⁻².

rubric.why: The work per unit time gives the pump’s power.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct power calculation.

rubric.why: Using g = 10 gives 1200 W; using g = 9.8 gives 1176 W.
rubric.description: States the power with its unit.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for 1200 W (taking g = 10 m s⁻²) or 1176 W (taking g = 9.8 m s⁻²).

modelAnswer: Given: m = 200 kg, h = 6 m, t = 10 s and g = 10 m s⁻².
Work done in lifting the water: W = mgh.
Power: P = W/t = mgh/t.
Substituting: P = (200 kg × 10 m s⁻² × 6 m)/(10 s) = 1200 W.
The power of the pump is 1200 W.

items.followUp: Define derived quantities and give two examples.

rubric.why: Derived quantities are defined using fundamental quantities.
rubric.description: States how derived quantities are formed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for saying that derived quantities are obtained by combining or defining them in terms of fundamental quantities.

rubric.why: Examples demonstrate quantities formed from fundamental quantities.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving at least one valid example, such as velocity, force, area, volume, density or acceleration.

modelAnswer: Derived quantities are physical quantities obtained by combining fundamental quantities by multiplication or division.
Examples include area, velocity, force and density.
